#329. Here’s Everything You Can Do With With the New Gemini AI on Android Auto

Google Assistant is being replaced by Google’s more advanced Gemini AI across all platforms, and that includes Android Auto. If the switch hasn’t happened yet on your own vehicle’s dashboard, then it should happen soon.

You’ll see a message onscreen announcing the arrival of Gemini, with the new “spark” icon (a small star by a sound-wave-like icon), instead of the traditional microphone when the AI is active.

If you've used Gemini before on your phone, on the web, or somewhere else, then you're going to know the extras that it brings over Google Assistant. It's a truly natural conversation partner that can dig deep into information available online, and respond to a much wider range of queries. Here's what the upgraded app can do specifically when you're traveling on the road.

All of the standard commands you might have already been using are still here, of course, like "navigate home" or “Where's the nearest Walmart?” With Gemini though, there's much more flexibility in what you can say without the AI getting confused or misunderstanding what you're asking about.

For example, your questions can be multilayered. Something like "find the nearest coffee shop that has a drive-thru and is open now" will look for those exact criteria. You're also able to ask context-sensitive follow-up questions, such as "What time will it shut?" or "How long will it take to get there?" if you need further details.

You can ask more general questions too, such as "tell me more about the place I'm heading to" or "Is there outdoor seating?” But bear in mind that Gemini will be limited to scouring the data on Google Maps for its information. (It's a disembodied AI that's never been anywhere.) If it doesn't know the answer to something, it should tell you that.

Overall, it's smarter in every aspect. I was recently navigating a difficult junction and couldn't work out whether the map was sending me left or right. I asked Gemini, "Will I be traveling east or west after the next turn?" and it figured out the answer. That helped me avoid veering off in the wrong direction.

One of the major benefits of having a voice-controlled AI in the car is having it handle messaging and audio tasks without you needing to take your eyes off the road or fish around for a button. If you tell Gemini to “read my last message,” it'll speak it out for you and give you the opportunity to reply. You can also specify the app, otherwise Google Messages will be used by default—Google Chat and WhatsApp are among the others that are supported.

Gemini is able to give you summaries of group chats, which is really handy when you're on a drive and the conversations you're involved in are building up message after message that you can't check. Name a group chat in a supported app and ask for a summary, or just request summaries of unread messages. You'll be able to get the gist without checking each individual message.

The usual array of audio commands are here, carried over from Google Assistant, so you can quickly start or stop audio in your music, podcast, radio, and audiobook apps. As well as continuing from where you left off, you can also name artists, albums, and playlists that you want to queue up. YouTube Music and Spotify are among the apps supported, if you need to specify one.

Another extra from Gemini is being able to ask about the artist or song that's currently playing, and get more information on it. You might want to learn the history of a particular band, find out how long a certain song was at number one, or even get recommendations based on what's currently playing—just ask Gemini.

Much more than Google Assistant, Gemini can help you learn something or develop some ideas while you're behind the wheel. If you're on the way to a movie premiere, you can ask Gemini about the history of the film, the director, and the actors, and it'll remember the context of your conversation. (It'll all get synced back to the Gemini app on your other devices.)

Voice commands such as “help me prepare for my interview” or “come up with ideas for a quick and easy meal to make for dinner" will initiate a chat with Gemini that you can continue throughout your journey—and hopefully arrive well-prepared or with dinner sorted (or whatever it is). Maybe don’t ask about anything too mind-bending, as you’ll still need to concentrate on driving.

Gemini will ask along the way for any information it needs about what you’re interviewing for or the ingredients you’ve got at home. You can also ask Gemini to quiz you on a certain topic or run a query on something you see on the journey—like a landmark or a restaurant you go past.

Finally, there’s always the weather: Gemini will give you forecasts for the areas and specific locations you give it, on whatever day you want within the next week or so. Perhaps more useful for journeys are questions like “When is the rain going to stop?” or “What are the weather conditions like at my destination?” which will help you plan your trip.

#328. Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'

Former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra: "It's going to be tough."

He should know. The 78-year-old businessman and U.S. Navy veteran helped with his own succession planning and recommended to GM's board in 2013 that Barra replace him as CEO. She has held the top job since Jan. 15, 2014.

Akerson said Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence, vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles.

"It's going to be very, very dynamic," Akerson told CNBC during a phone interview. "It's going to be a big change."

Akerson declined to discuss potential internal candidates such as GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson, CFO Paul Jacobson or President Mark Reuss, but he said the eventual successor needs to be dynamic and, if from the outside, "adaptable."

His comments to CNBC follow a Wall Street Journal report on Tuesday that GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside candidates to succeed Barra, in addition to internal prospects. GM declined to comment on the report or Barra's succession.

Akerson, who came to GM as an outsider from The Carlyle Group in 2010, said selecting an outside candidate might be risky if there are already executives within the organization who have similar leadership and technical expertise.

"Is there anybody in the organization that has that background that you know better day to day over a period of time? You may be taking a risk by bringing in an outsider," he said.

The prospect of an outsider leading GM would be unusual in the auto industry, where major automakers have generally promoted internal CEO candidates, apart from periods of exceptional disruption such as the Great Recession.

Stellantis, BMW, Toyota Motor, Nissan Motor and Hyundai Motor have all appointed internal executives to their CEO positions in recent years.

Barra has said several times that her successor and her longevity in the role would be determined by the board.

A notable influence is likely Hewlett Packard veteran Patricia Russo, GM's longest-serving board member who has been on the board since 2009 and leads its CEO succession planning as independent lead director.

GM's CEO succession planning is done "at least annually," according to the company's yearly proxy filing. That process includes Barra providing the board "with recommendations for, and evaluations of, potential CEO successors and discusses developmental plans for these successors," according to the filing.

That is followed by board members engaging "with CEO candidates and senior management talent at Board and committee meetings and other forums to enable directors to personally assess candidates."

When Akerson was preparing to retire, Barra was among a pool of four candidates — two longtime GM employees and two relative newcomers — who were finalists for CEO in 2013, he said.

Akerson said he put the finalists through an extended evaluation, asking how they viewed GM's strengths and weaknesses, how they would organize the company, and their willingness to work together, potentially with other CEO candidates who didn't get the job.

Akerson said the final decision to appoint Barra was done at a day-and-a-half-long board meeting in Washington. The candidate field was narrowed to Barra and former GM executive Dan Ammann, an ex-Wall Street banker who was GM's CFO before leaving the automaker's Cruise unit, reportedly over a disagreement in strategy with Barra, in 2021.

"Mary's very deserving of all the accolades she's received," Akerson said. "She's done a terrific job."

Barra has been leading the automaker for nearly 13 years, which makes her the longest-serving CEO of the automaker since Alfred Sloan retired after a 23-year career as CEO in 1946.

Akerson said he believes that, like he did, Barra will have major influence in picking her successor. He described that dynamic as integral to continuing her legacy leading the automaker.

"This is important. I think if she doesn't pick the right person, in four or five years from now and things are back in the trough, that will tarnish her history. But I think she'll pick the right one," he said.

#327. Target is giving away free gift cards worth up to $1,000 on Black Friday: How to claim

TL;DR: On Black Friday (Nov. 27), the first 100 guests in line at every Target store get a free $25, $50, or $100 Target gift card — plus one $1,000 winner per store (no purchase necessary).

Target is giving early birds a major incentive to set their alarms on Black Friday morning. On Friday, Nov. 27, the retailer is handing out free Target gift cards worth $25, $50, or $100 to the first 100 eligible guests in line at every store — plus one lucky shopper at each location will walk away with a $1,000 Target gift card.

Unlike online doorbusters that disappear in seconds, this giveaway happens strictly in person and comes with a tight arrival and redemption window.

Target stores reopen at 6 a.m. local time on Black Friday, Nov. 27. Showing up right at 6 a.m. will be too late if you want a free gift card. Target associates will start handing out prize redemption tickets to the first 100 eligible people in line roughly an hour before doors open (around 5 a.m. local time at most stores).

Tickets are handed out on a first-come, first-served basis while supplies last, with a strict limit of one ticket per person.

Once doors open at 6 a.m. local time, you have to take your ticket to the Black Friday event cart inside that same Target store within one hour of store opening (by 7 a.m. local time at 6 a.m. locations). If you miss that one-hour redemption window, you forfeit your prize.

Your card's exact dollar value is revealed when you redeem your ticket at the event cart. Out of the 100 winners at every store, 60 people get a $25 gift card, 30 get a $50 gift card, nine get a $100 gift card, and one person gets the $1,000 grand prize.

The giveaway is open to shoppers ages 13 and older (minors need a parent or legal guardian's permission to participate), and no purchase is necessary to get a ticket or claim a card.

Once you claim your gift card, you can spend it right away on Target's Black Friday sale or save it for later in stores and online — just note that you cannot use it on prepaid or specialty gift cards. Anything you buy that's eligible also qualifies for Target's Holiday Price Match Guarantee through Dec. 24.

Double-check your local Target's exact hours before heading out — and if you are mapping out a multi-store morning route, check out our guide to Black Friday 2026 store hours to see when other major retailers open their doors.

#326. Pizza chains are under pressure. GLP-1 use is only one part of the problem

Big pizza chains are struggling as weaker consumer spending, a wider variety of dining options and the rise of GLP-1 medications weigh on their sales.

The pandemic was a boom time for Domino's Pizza, Papa Johns, Little Caesars and Pizza Hut. But since dining rooms reopened, the biggest U.S. pizza chains have faced an uphill battle to retain their customers.

These days, consumers are watching their discretionary spending but have more delivery and takeout options when they do decide to order, thanks to the accessibility of third-party platforms. Plus, food quality and the customer experience have become more important to diners who are looking for value when they order from restaurants.

As a result of pizza fatigue and challenges facing the broader restaurant industry, the number of U.S. pizza restaurants has tumbled. Since pizza locations hit a peak of 83,035 nationwide in August 2019, more than 9,600 pizzerias had closed their doors as of July 2026, according to data from Datassential.

In 2025, sales at U.S. pizza restaurants fell 0.3%, according to Technomic data. Sales at independent pizzerias slipped 0.4%. Chains, which account for about two-thirds of the domestic pizza category sales, saw revenue shrink 0.3%.

Papa Johns reported that North American same-store sales declined 2.5% in 2025. Pizza Hut's U.S. same-store sales fell 5%. Among the three pizza chains that were publicly traded last year, only Domino's posted annual same-store sales growth at its U.S. restaurants, with an increase of 3%.

It isn't just diners who have lost their appetite for pizza. Since March 2020, Papa Johns stock has lost about two-thirds of its value. Even shares of Domino's, which dominates the category, have seen gains of only about 2% in that time. For comparison, the S&P 500 has climbed about 150% over the same period.

And Yum Brands sold Pizza Hut this year, offloading the laggard of its portfolio to LongRange Capital and Yum China after about two decades of stagnating sales.

"Pizza Hut has been a detractor for YUM ... Going forward, YUM won't be tripped up by pizza category dynamics (discounting, etc.), translating to stronger growth and higher concentration in higher growth industry segments and markets," Wells Fargo analyst Zachary Fadem wrote in a research note in September.

Pizza chains now have significantly more competition for diners' dollars than they did in 2020. Third-party delivery platforms, which grew in popularity during the pandemic, offer a wide variety of cuisines beyond the traditional pizza and Chinese. As a result, Domino's and Papa John's have to compete with other fast-food chains, like McDonald's and Chick-fil-A, for DoorDash and Uber Eats orders.

As pizza has grown more expensive, a pie seems less appealing to budget-conscious diners. The average large cheese pizza is now almost $17, according to the 2026 Pizza Power Report from PMQ Pizza, a trade publication.

Plus, frozen pizza is another convenient option, with a lower price tag. Retail sales of single- and multi-serve frozen pizza rose 2.9% in the 52 weeks ended Nov. 7 compared with the same period in 2022, according to NielsenIQ data.

"When the American consumer is focused on the least expensive eating occasion, the items that are in my pantry, my refrigerator and my freezer win every single time," said David Portalatin, a food and food service industry advisor for Circana.

Convenience stores like Casey's General Stores have also won over customers with pizza at a low price point.

"We believe that [Casey's] has an advantage over [quick-service restaurants] and dollar stores, which have fewer options to navigate the persistent inflationary environment, while [Casey's] can offset food pressures with margins," Bank of America Securities analyst Sara Senatore wrote in a research note published in June.

She added that geographic overlap of locations suggests that Casey's is stealing share from Pizza Hut.

The biggest pizza chains have also been slow to adapt to shifting consumer attitudes toward nutrition. For example, of the four biggest chains, Papa Johns is the only one to even test a pizza crust with added protein as more diners prioritize it in their diets. And the test was only in one Atlanta restaurant — for a single day.

Pizza's nutritional content more broadly is another drag for the category. Its carbohydrate and fat content, from its dough and cheese, respectively, can make it less appealing for consumers on GLP-1 drugs, which have skyrocketed in use over the last several years.

Spending on pizza quick-service restaurants has fallen 22.2% per GLP-1 household after six to eight months using the medications, according to a 2026 survey published by PwC.

To be sure, pizza's recent struggles do not mean an existential crisis for the category. Total pizza servings are down only about 1% this year, Circana's Portalatin said.

And chains are trying to reverse that downturn in servings. In August, Domino's launched the Domino, a customizable Detroit-style personal pizza to attract solo diners. In November, Papa Johns unveiled a new turnaround plan focusing on improving food consistency and restaurant operations. And Pizza Hut is running a holiday-themed meal deal.

"Pizza's not going anywhere," Portalatin said. "The American consumer loves pizza."

#325. CAS reinstates Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions

The Court of Arbitration for Sport has reinstated Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions, overturning a CAF decision that stripped them of the title. Morocco, previously declared winners, are confirmed runners-up.

Just over eight months after Senegal were stripped of their 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON) title, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has announced that Senegal's appeal has been upheld, reinstating them as 2025 AFCON winners. Morocco, who had been declared champions after a Confederation of African Football (CAF) review, has now been confirmed as runners-up.

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French)," the CAS statement read.

"The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed."

The statement continued that it felt "the Referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority" and that his "decision was covered by the ‘field of play’ doctrine."

The decision comes after a closed-doors hearing at CAS' headquarters in Lausanne in early October.

Before the verdict was delivered, Morocco captain Achraf Hakimi posted a message on Instagram saying he would disagree with Senegal being stripped of the title because "its players fought so hard to win."

"I respect the authorities responsible for football, but I firmly believe that what happens on the pitch should be the most important thing of all. Senegal won that Africa Cup of Nations final through their performance, their determination, and the effort of every player, just as every player represents his country. They fought for that title, and no one can erase what those players achieved on the pitch," Hakimi wrote.

"African football needs unity, fairness, and credibility. We cannot keep building our game if decisions like these leave players and fans questioning everything."

The final was played on January 18, with Senegal winning 1-0 after extra-time. However, the game was thrown into confusion when many Senegal players walked off the pitch following the referee's decision to award Morocco a penalty in the final minutes. Around 15 minutes later, and after furious Senegalese fans had attempted a pitch invasion, the players did return. Morocco's Brahim Diaz inexplicably missed the penalty, sending the game into extra time, which is when Senegal scored the eventual winner.

Just 10 days afterwards, the CAF issued fines worth more than $1 million (€835,000) and banned players from both teams.

Two months later, and after the Senegal team had paraded the trophy to their fans, CAF declared that Senegal had "forfeited" the final by leaving the pitch. CAF then overturned the result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory and the title. The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) denounced the CAF decision and took the case to CAS.

The aftermath had rumbled on for months, with many believing it damaging for African football as a whole.

"If you look at it critically, the value of African football will definitely go down with this," Collins Okinyo, a former CAF media consultant, told DW after the result had been overturned in March.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The ruling brings an end to a saga that had cast a cloud over a well-organized tournament in Morocco.

The country is emerging as a major football hub in Africa. Already confirmed as a co-host for the World Cup in 2030, Morocco also hosted the 2026 Women's AFCON and has been hosting the U17 Women's World Cup annually since 2025 and is set to do so until 2029. It is further rumored that the Morocco, along with fellow 2030 World Cup hosts Spain and Portugal, is keen to host the next Club World Cup in 2029 as a form of preparation ahead of the big event in 2030.

Although it has made significant advances in sports infrastructure, not everyone is happy about Morocco's push into the football world. In 2025, there were major protests by Gen Z questioning the country's priorities in light of struggling health and education systems.

#324. This boiled bag of offal is banned in the US. In Scotland it's a fine-dining treat

Anthony Bourdain loved haggis. But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.

“Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain said on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow. “There is no more unfairly reviled food on Earth than the haggis.”

A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.

Instagrammable is not the word that immediately comes to mind. In our 21st-century world, where “clean” eating and processed pap overlap, haggis can seem like an “Outlander”-style outlier from another age.

Yet, by some alchemy, once cooked to its required “warm-reekin’ (steaming)” state, it adds up to much more than the sum of its modest parts. It’s offaly charm has kept nose-to-tail eating alive among a younger generation of Scots that has largely turned its back on the tripe, liver and kidneys their predecessors enjoyed (or endured).

Carefully prepared, haggis tastes both oaty and meaty; it is dark and crumbly, a little crispy at the edges but still moist; earthy but also savory and spicy; deep-tasting and profoundly warming, the perfect foil for its traditional garnish of floury mashed potatoes and orange bashed turnip.

“It’s like a cuddle for the stomach,” says Nicola Turner, a 35-year-old office administrator from Helensburgh, a town on western Scotland’s Firth of Clyde.

For children of the 1960s and ’70s, like crime novelist Ian Rankin, haggis meals were a choice between the classic meat-and-two-veg plate and the battered and deep-fried, chip-shop iteration loved by both his friend Bourdain and his quintessentially Scottish detective character, Inspector John Rebus.

Now myriad other treatments have blossomed.

“I’m pretty sure the first time I dined with AB in Edinburgh we had haggis in filo pastry with a jam-style – maybe blackcurrant – sauce,” Rankin recalled. “He was a big fan of haggis and of chip shops. Rebus will have enjoyed the occasional haggis supper from his local chip shop. He was definitely a fan, as am I.”

“It is all about the spicing and the texture,” says the Scottish food writer, novelist and cook Sue Lawrence, a champion of haggis’ adaptability for use in other dishes. “If you didn’t know what was in it, you wouldn’t think ‘oh that tastes of liver or whatever.’ It is all nicely chopped up and the oatmeal gives it a lovely texture. It could easily be a nice, big mince dish.”

These US restaurants and chefs are James Beard Award finalists

Lawrence uses haggis as an alternative to beef and pork ragù in lasagna and in her pastilla, a version of the North African dish in which a hand-made haggis from the Isle of Mull substitutes for the traditional poultry or seafood filling. The filo pastry savory is flavored with the spice blend ras el hanout, apricots, chile, orange zest and almonds before being sprinkled with cinnamon and icing sugar.

Such cultural crossovers serve as a reminder that haggis could easily be a dish with nothing specifically Scottish about it at all. Records of similar quick and portable preparations of the fast-perishing innards of sheep and other animals date back to ancient Rome and Greece.

Haggis-like combinations of offal and grains are part of the culinary history of several countries. Spain has chireta, Romania drob and Sweden polsa, while chaudin, or ponce, is a rice and meat-stuffed pig stomach that is a staple of Cajun cooking.

In neighboring England, recipes for “hagese,” “hagws of a schepe,” “haggas” or “haggus” pop up in recipe books published between the 15th and 17th centuries, probably preceding written records north of the border.

Etymological evidence points to the term “haggis” having its roots in Old Norse, suggesting an early version of an oat-and-offal sausage might have arrived in Britain and Ireland on a Viking longboat.

But ever since it was first optioned by the poet Robert Burns in the late 1700s, the haggis backstory has been monopolized by Scotland and the Scots, sometimes mischievously.

It is, according to the kind of lore that Burns engendered, the dish a doughty Highlander would carry with him as he drove cattle through the glens to the markets of the central belt or the perfect picnic for a whisky smuggler plying his illicit trade by moonlight.

From such romantic notions it was a short step to turning the haggis into a wee wild beastie, one with longer legs on one side that was thus condemned to run round and round whichever hill it lived on. In 2003, a poll of American tourists in Scotland found that one in three of them believed they might encounter such a confused creature on a Caledonian vacation.

Bourdain, a native New Yorker, may have qualified as haggis’ biggest admirer since Burns, but his compatriots at the US Department of Agriculture remain unconverted to offal-filled paunch. Haggis imports into the United States were prohibited in 1971 as part of a ban on the consumption of all livestock lungs. Authentic versions of old school haggis remain culinary contraband in the US, as hard to lay your hands on as Cuban cigars.

Across the rest of the world, it’s a different story. According to leading producer Simon Howie, haggis is more widely appreciated and consumed now than it has been since Burns improvised his “Address to a Haggis” for the entertainment of well-to-do Edinburgh acquaintances.

Firmly tongue-in-cheek, the poem lauds the “Great chieftain o’ the pudding race,” as exactly the kind of unpretentious, hearty fare required to nourish a nation of braveheart warriors.

In comparison to the enfeebling foreign muck enjoyed by the capital’s claret-quaffing elites of the time – the olio, fricassée or ragoût that would “sicken a sow” – Burns urges his readers to wonder at the magical impact of haggis on his fellow sons of Scotland’s soil.

As the English translation of the original Scots language version puts it:

These days synthetic casings have largely replaced stomach but ovine and porcine innards remain at the core of most of the haggis produced in its homeland, said Howie, who estimates that his company Simon Howie Butchers, accounts for around 60% of the roughly two million haggises produced every year.

For Howie, versatility, value for money and convenience explain why this staple of the Scottish larder is thriving. Typically haggis retails in Scotland, which accounts for half of global consumption by volume, for around £6, or $7.70 per kilogram ($3.36/pound). That’s around half the price of less expensive cuts of beef or a third of the price of Scotch lamb while enjoying a fairly similar nutritional and calorific profile.

“You can give your kids a meal that is not full of things you don’t want to feed them – for a few pounds you can feed three strapping lads,” Howie said.

“From a kitchen perspective, it is very simple because when it leaves our factory it is already cooked. So when you or a restaurant owner gets it into the kitchen all you have to do is heat it up to be piping hot. It couldn’t be more basic: a student with no cooking skills or a Michelin-starred chef do exactly the same thing to put it out on the plate.”

Its texture means haggis can also be usefully deployed in fine dining alongside leaner meat like venison or as a stuffing for poultry and game birds. Its spicy intensity means it is also finding uses in canapés and as a crouton-borne garnish for soups.

Buoyant sales are also underpinned by the increasing consumption of haggis in forms inspired by Scotland’s ethnic minorities.

Glasgow’s Sikh community pioneered haggis pakora in the 1990s and samosas, spring rolls and quesadillas have followed in its wake, often using a vegetarian version of the protein in which the offal is replaced by a mix of vegetables, pulses and mushrooms.

Such dishes are more than culinary twists. They are badges of belonging, and an indication that, two centuries after Burns grabbed it for the nation, haggis is as intimately entwined with Scots identity as ever.

Just ask Ross O’Cinneide, a promising 14-year-old fly-half in the junior section of Stirling County rugby club.

“Most of my friends and I like haggis,” he says. “Mum makes it for us sometimes after rugby and it’s got a very nice warming feeling. And it’s nice because it’s purely Scottish.”

#323. The Best MagSafe Wallets for Your Everyday Carry (2026)

The best MagSafe wallets are compact, slim, and svelte, and they attach securely to your iPhone (or MagSafe-compatible case). They are handy if you only want to carry a few cards, like your work badge or train fare. MagSafe wallets are also great for anyone who wants to travel light and forgo a traditional wallet entirely. We’ve tested dozens, and our favorites are below.

Read our MagSafe guides for more useful accessory recommendations, including the Best MagSafe Accessories, Best MagSafe Power Banks, Best MagSafe Wireless Chargers, and Best MagSafe Grips.

Updated November 2026: I’ve added new wallets to our honorable mentions section and removed discontinued products. I’ve also checked for accuracy throughout.

MagSafe is Apple’s magnetic technology built into the iPhone 12, iPhone 13, iPhone 14, iPhone 15, iPhone 16 (excluding the iPhone 16e), iPhone 17, iPhone 18 Pro, and iPhone Duo. It features a hidden ring of magnets on the back of the phone and was developed to create a faster, more precise wireless charging system. Those magnets also connect to accessories such as external batteries, car mounts, and wallets.

If you use a case on your iPhone, make sure it’s also MagSafe (the case will have a ring of magnets inside). This will ensure a proper connection with MagSafe accessories. If you use a non-MagSafe case, the connection will be very weak, and MagSafe products may just slide off your iPhone. We have lots of case recommendations in our guides:

When buying a wallet, make sure it supports MagSafe or Qi2 connections. The product description should indicate this prominently. Qi2 is the wireless charging standard, and all MagSafe iPhones support Qi2. Android phones now also support Qi2, and some have magnets inside, like the Google Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 series (Google calls it Pixelsnap).

MagSafe wallets use the same ring of magnets that lets them snap directly onto the back of the iPhone or a MagSafe- or supported Qi2 case. This gives the wallet a strong and secure hold on your device. The wallets we’ve included in this guide all have the MagSafe seal of approval.

Apple first introduced MagSafe for its iPhones in 2020. The following models support the technology:

Do MagSafe Wallets Work With Android Phones?

To use a MagSafe wallet with an Android phone (or the iPhone 16e), you’ll need to use a MagSafe case. Several case manufacturers have started adding a ring of magnets to Android phone cases to bring the same magnetic experience native to iPhones.

Will a MagSafe Wallet Demagnetize My Credit Card?

No, MagSafe will not demagnetize your credit cards. Credit cards have magnetic stripe encoding strong enough to resist demagnetization, and the MagSafe wallets in this guide include a built-in shield designed to keep your cards safe. However, you may run into issues with hotel key cards and some gift cards. Keep those away as a precaution.

I use a MagSafe wallet every day as my primary wallet. I check that it snaps firmly onto the iPhone or MagSafe case—and that it doesn’t slide off when I take my phone out of my pocket, bag, or jacket. I also make sure cards fit well in the sleeve and don’t fall out. I only recommend wallets that feel durable, are easy to use, and can hold the standard amount of cards (at least two to three). I occasionally call on my fellow WIRED reviewers for long-term testing or to check out new models.

UAG’s Metropolis MagSafe wallet is on the spendier side, but you won’t be replacing it in a year or two. It is lightweight yet robust with Kevlar construction. There’s a large slot on the back that can hold up to three cards, and you can unfold the wallet and store an additional three (or cash) inside. It also pulls double duty as a stand if you need to prop up your phone, and you can orient your phone in landscape or portrait mode. —Molly Higgins

Smartish’s MagSafe wallet makes me wish all wallets had a slot on the side to push out the cards. I never had to take it off my phone to access cards. Just give the spacious side opening a little push with your thumb, and the cards slide out. My cards remained secure, and I never had an issue with them falling out. It’s made of vegan leather, and Smartish offers a few fun designs. —Brenda Stolyar

This luxe, super-thin leather MagSafe wallet from Nomad has Apple’s Find My feature built in, so you can easily locate it in the Find My app if it’s misplaced. That does mean you need to charge the wallet, but don’t worry, there's no proprietary cable here. Instead, the wallet can be wirelessly charged on any MagSafe or Qi2 charger; once it’s fully charged, the battery lasts for five months. Easy peasy.

It’s made from vegetable-tanned Horween leather with a polycarbonate frame, and it can hold up to four cards. (A less expensive version that uses Nomad's Camino leather is also available.) It looks classy, and it’s great for anyone with a tendency to lose things. —Molly Higgins

Note that Nomad also sells a dedicated tracker card, which can add Find My to any wallet but will take up valuable space in a MagSafe version.

I love this wallet from Moft, which is compatible with Apple Find My, so you always know where it is. It’s relatively standard-looking, but it has a built-in tripod, which came in handy numerous times when I wanted to film a quick outfit check or take a group photo. It raises your phone camera to 8 inches high, and the wallet is very sturdy, so you can dial in the right angle. It works in landscape or portrait orientation. With space for two cards, it isn’t the roomiest but is rich in features. —Louryn Strampe

You can always rely on Casetify for unique designs. Its Snappy MagSafe wallet is available in various styles and colors. It’s slim, durable, and sleek—the illustrations haven’t faded after months of use. It’s made from vegan leather (aka plastic), but Casetify uses BioVeg, derived from recycled polyester and vegetable oil from non-food and GMO-free corn crops.

It can hold up to three cards, and there’s a built-in shield that protects them from magnetic damage. My only gripe is that it can be a little difficult to pull the cards out when the wallet is attached to your phone or case. I typically have to detach it and use the opening from the back to slide out the cards. —Brenda Stolyar

Ridge’s metal MagSafe wallet feels solid and high-quality. A few of us tested it, and it reliably held our setups, including one tester’s daily carry of eight cards plus a thicker tracking card. The magnets could be stronger, but Ridge does sell a strengthening tray that might be useful if you’re concerned.

This wallet can be a little weird to use at first, but you build up muscle memory quickly. There’s a finger slot for pushing cards out, and you slide them back in on the opposite side. Ridge also includes a Torx screwdriver and extra screws, which are useful for switching out the plates, adding or subtracting room for cards, or adding on accessories like the brand’s wallet chain or cash strap. —Louryn Strampe

Most MagSafe wallets are designed to hold just a few cards, but I love the Moft Snap Field because it can hold so much more. You get plenty of storage space for cards—technically up to eight cards, though more reasonably seven—alongside a dedicated slot for an extra SIM card and a SIM card ejector.

That extra room already puts the Snap Field a step ahead of most other MagSafe wallets, but you can also store just about anything you want inside. It uses a folding design held together by magnets, so you can quickly throw in cash, coins, or paper cards. Regardless of what you store inside, you can easily get to your cards with a pull tab. And, if all of that wasn’t enough, the backing that attaches to your phone can pop out and function as a kickstand. —Jacob Roach

ESR’s MagSafe wallet isn’t bulky, but it also isn’t so thin that it feels insubstantial. It doubles as a kickstand and sticks to my phone reliably. There’s space for five cards—three in the external pockets, plus another two on the inside. I really like the clear window that keeps my ID separate and handy to flash when I get carded. This wallet is simple, but that’s the beauty of it, and it’s affordable to boot. If you want something basic, it’s a good option to consider. Just keep in mind that the included RFID-blocking card probably isn’t necessary. —Louryn Strampe

Casely’s wallet is made of hard silicone, so it’s slightly heavier and thicker than the other ones I’ve tested. It feels similar to having a MagSafe battery pack on the back. I don’t mind the extra weight and thickness because it makes it easier to grip my phone case. There’s a dedicated slot at the bottom that makes sliding cards out a breeze. Just know that if you pair it with the complementary Casely case, the whole thing is bulky. But darn if it doesn’t look cute. —Brenda Stolyar

I’m obsessed with PopSockets grips—I have one on my phone and one on my Kindle. If you’re also a fan and don’t want to get rid of the accessory with a MagSafe wallet, well, you don’t have to. The Popwallet+ is both a PopSockets grip and a wallet. It fits up to three cards (or more, depending on the thickness), and the cloth opening at the bottom makes it easy to push out the cards. The grip works the same way a standard one does, with the ability to expand and collapse. You can swap out the tops if you ever get bored with the design. —Brenda Stolyar

Supcase’s MagFlip wallet and stand is extremely sturdy, and feels unbreakable. It’s constructed almost entirely out of metal, fitted with huge magnets that never let go and thick hinges around the body. You can store up to five cards in the wallet itself, and there’s an RFID-blocking card that sits at the end, though this kind of protection is largely unnecessary.

It doubles as a two-height stand as well. You can kick the wallet back and prop your phone up, but if you rotate the wallet around, you can position your phone even higher with a kickstand that keeps everything stable. Even with the rugged, almost militarized construction, SupCase still offers a handful of attractive colors, including one that combines a faux leather exterior with regal gold accents. —Jacob Roach

A lot of MagSafe wallets just feel like a pocket on the back of your phone. This one from ESR feels like an actual wallet. It comes in a variety of stylish options with a slick metal-tipped clasp and detailed construction. There’s a clear window for your ID, a roomy card pocket, and a compartment that can hold two bills. The card compartment can technically hold up to four cards, but I prefer two or three for easier access. If you want space for cash as well as the other essentials, or you want a leather-type wallet that has more design choices than some competitors, I recommend this one. —Louryn Strampe

Looks like you need some MagSafe for your MagSafe. Look no further than the Valentinus wallet from Spigen. It’s constructed out of polyurethane leather and can technically hold three cards (I’m able to easily fit four). It comes with a handy card cutout at the bottom so you can quickly thumb through them. The real draw is an extra MagSafe ring built into the back of the wallet.

Stack a MagSafe grip on the back, mount your phone to a MagSafe car stand, or attach whatever other MagSafe accessory you want; you don’t need to take off your wallet first. You can’t charge your phone through it, but the convenience of using other accessories while keeping your wallet attached is worth the price of admission. —Jacob Roach

Moft’s Snap-on Phone Stand and Wallet is another good kickstand wallet option. You can set it up at three angles: one for scrolling through your phone, one for streaming media, and one for video conferencing. It feels sturdy, and the case isn’t bulky. I wouldn’t put more than two cards in this one, though. I usually use it to carry my license and debit card, while the rest are in my Apple Wallet. —Brenda Stolyar

Alternatively, Moft sells a trackable version with Apple Find My capabilities. It even comes in versions that can match your iPhone. It isn’t super roomy, but I still like it.

ESR Geo Wallet Stand for $47: Apple’s Find My app lets you track your devices if they’re lost, and ESR’s Geo wallet has it built right into the wallet itself. This is the wallet I’ve been using for the past few weeks, and outside of its Find My capabilities, I love that it strikes a great balance between size and usability. ESR says it can hold up to three cards, but I’ve been using mine with four—three cards plus my ID—and I can get them all out easily. Although having a wallet with magnetic charging pins is weird—the Find My feature requires a battery that lasts three months—you can turn it off if you don’t care for it (but then, maybe just buy a different wallet). It does kind of suck that you need a proprietary charger to recharge your wallet, though. The magnets adhere well to the back of the phone, and you can pop open the wallet and use it as a kickstand. ESR even includes a strap on the back that works as a phone grip.

OtterBox Symmetry Series Cactus Leather MagSafe Wallet for $45: This wallet is nice and simple, thin, lightweight, has a strong hold on my phone case, and offers a dedicated fabric-covered slot at the bottom to push the cards out (I was able to fit three without much trouble). This OtterBox wallet is made from cactus-based leather, which feels nearly as luxurious as real leather. Just know that cactus leather isn’t as eco-friendly as it’s made out to be—these cases are still infused with layers of plastic.

Spigen MagSafe Classic LS Wallet for $40: This cool-looking wallet incorporates design inspiration from the classic Macintosh computers. The gray might seem a little bit drab, but any Apple enthusiast will likely enjoy the nod to the computers of yesteryear. It’s otherwise pretty standard fare, with space for up to three cards. I like the thumb notch, which makes it easy to slide your cards out.

Pelican Protector MagSafe Wallet: This MagSafe wallet is simply too bulky. It’s difficult to slip into a pocket, and we don’t think the protective hardshell is worth the trade-off since it can only hold two or three cards.

Kate Spade New York Morgan MagSafe Wallet: This wallet looks nice, but the finish starts to degrade with regular use. It also opened on its own once or twice, which left me worried about a card slipping out.

Ohsnap! Snap Grip Wallet: I had high hopes for this one, mainly because of its build quality. The wallet is aluminum, can hold up to eight cards (depending on whether they have raised lettering or not), has MagSafe support, and comes with a grip that doubles as a kickstand. Unfortunately, the grip is made of plastic, and it broke after a short time (it won’t fold properly back into place). The magnetic hold isn’t as strong as other MagSafe wallets, even with a MagSafe-approved case on my phone. None of that is great, especially at this high price.

Apple FineWoven MagSafe Case: Any time this wallet is separated from your iPhone, you’ll get an alert and can track it in Apple’s Find My app. It has a single slot that fits up to three cards, but to remove them, you have to take it off your iPhone and push the cards up through the slot on the back. Unfortunately, Apple’s MagSafe wallets use only the company’s proprietary FineWoven material (made from recycled materials). It’s a commendable effort to reduce reliance on leather production, but several WIRED reviewers have said the material doesn’t hold up well over time.

Journey Loc8 Universal MagSafe Slim Wallet: My cards would slip out of this wallet if I didn’t have it stuffed full, which makes it an obvious “Do Not Recommend” choice when so many other comparable wallets don’t have this problem.

#322. International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin

The era of U.S. airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed. In its place will be a massive business-class cabin with room for 70 passengers.

U.S. airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a new top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines have already taken this step. American was the last of the U.S. airlines to still have first class on long-haul international routes.

Many travelers might not notice the difference. That's because of airlines' investments into business class: new suites, bigger screens, better technology like device-charging pads, and improved bedding.

It's part of airlines' big bet on mass luxury. Consumers have been willing to shell out more to fly comfortably, which is helping to boost airline revenue. That's all the more important as costs of everything from fuel to airport landing fees have been rising, soaking up more of the industry's profits.

The retirement of first class ends a more-than-six-decade stretch of the jet age that in the early days included service like seat-side carving of chateaubriand and meals served on fine bone china.

A few decades ago, business class was much smaller, with two-by-two seats in some configurations, and recliners, not the lie-flat seats that dominate those cabins now.

"When you've got individual pods in biz class, and you've got a comfortable enough seat and bedding and decent wine, for a lot of people this is good enough," said Henry Harteveldt, founder of travel consulting firm Atmosphere Research Group and a former airline executive.

The over-the-top dining of the early days of international first class was a form of entertainment, long before laptops, personal seat-back screens and in-flight Wi-Fi, or even the promise of sleep on lie-flat beds, but customers still eat lots on board, Harteveldt said.

"People say they want to sleep but then they stay up and they eat every morsel," he said. "They're hypocrites."

There was still a hefty price gap between first and business.

A flight between Los Angeles and London on American's Boeing 777-300ER this week went for $12,994 in business class for a one-way ticket and $15,669 for a first-class seat.

American's last flight with international first class departed Friday morning local time in Sydney, bound for Los Angeles.

Its new cabin on its Boeing 777-300ERs will feature 70 business-class suites, the most of any U.S. airline. Pre-overhaul, the cabins had been operating with eight first-class suites and 52 pods in business, though the remodeling is ongoing. American is also flying a subfleet of 787-9 Dreamliners that have 51 business-class suites. (United is putting 64 new suites on that aircraft.)

Part of the allure is that some companies allow employees to book business-class tickets, but not first class.

American Airlines told CNBC it's growing its business-class cabins across the fleet. It's evaluating increasing the number of suites on its smaller long-haul jets, the Boeing 787-8 Dreamliners, from 20 currently to somewhere in the 30s.

"You don't have enough seats to make the seat cost competitive," Nat Pieper, American's chief commercial officer, said in an interview this month. "So what you need to do to make that airplane work is it's got to be a yield play. You need more business-class seats."

Differences between first and business classes on American lately came down to details.

On American's first-class long-haul section, passengers got olives with warm nuts to accompany their beverage early in the flight, while there were no olives for business class.

First class got a soup; business did not. First class got a warm dessert served a la mode in addition to the cold dessert or fruit and cheese plate both cabins were offered.

And there was no memory foam lumbar pillow for business class like there was in first, American said. But otherwise, the experiences were fairly similar for passengers. They still got better food options and service than economy passengers, along with their bigger seats, early boarding and lounge access.

"It's not like the bed can go any flatter than 180 degrees," Harteveldt said. "The bedding can be thicker, and the food nicer."

Delta and United have already replaced international, long-haul first class with dozens of their Delta One and Polaris business lie-flat suites, respectively, each of which is getting upgrades now.

American will continue offering a separate lie-flat first class on its Airbus A321T subfleet it uses for domestic cross-country flying until early 2027. But then that goes away, too.

Meanwhile, airlines over the past decade have added a premium economy section, which sits between business class and economy. It features recliner seats similar to those in domestic first class, often with foot rests, meals served on actual plates, larger seat-back screens than economy and earlier boarding.

Airlines are now cutting up business class into different segments, something they've done for more than a decade with the coach cabin's basic economy, standard and extra legroom seats.

United and Delta this year each announced their most expensive cabins will be sold with basic options, which are more restrictive and don't include things like the ability to pick your seat ahead of time or get access to a special airport lounge.

There are also a few seats in some of the business-class cabins that are roomier, like American's Flagship Suite Preferred and United's Polaris Studio. Even the guest seating in the United suite varies with "standard and companion ottomans," the latter including a seatbelt so you can ask "another Polaris passenger to visit you between takeoff and landing for a drink, chat or game," the airline says.

"I don't think we found the limit on segmentation," United CFO Mike Leskinen told CNBC on Thursday. "We have a few things on the drawing board. We're not done."

Although U.S. carriers are moving away from the designation, first class is far from dead.

Singapore Airlines, Germany's Lufthansa, British Airways and Air France have unveiled updated first-class cabins and other service improvements like food.

British Airways last month said it will build a record 106-suite business class on its Airbus A380 aircraft, the world's largest passenger airplane, but it's also upgrading its first class on board.

Meanwhile, smaller airlines like JetBlue Airways, Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air are introducing domestic or short-haul first-class seats.

"We're going to be able to do that at a really low price comparatively to what you're used to out there in the marketplace," Frontier Chief Commercial Officer Bobby Schroeter said last month.

#320. EU enlargement: Why do some EU member states use their vetoes to block the accession of certain candidate countries?

Individual EU member states use their veto powers to block candidate countries in the accession process — often for reasons of domestic politics. DW takes a look at some cases and examines what's behind them.

It's been quite a while since the European Union's last enlargement, when Croatia joined the bloc back in 2013.

If everything goes according to plan, another might soon be on the cards: Montenegro, with a population of just 620,000, could complete accession negotiations in the coming months and join the EU in early 2028.

But no sooner had EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos made this announcement in October than news emerged that Croatia might veto Montenegro's accession unless the country meets a series of Croatian demands. EU politicians and MEPs were dismayed.

This is not the first time something like this has happened: The veto rights that member states have on many EU matters have increasingly been used by individual countries in recent years as a means of leverage or obstruction, paralyzing the EU in the process.

DW takes a look at some of the most significant cases, the background to them and what are — in some instances — the serious political consequences of them.

Montenegro is the most advanced EU candidate country, with a potential accession date of 2028. It has already provisionally closed several of the EU's 33 negotiating chapters.

As of November 23, however, Croatia is blocking the closure of three chapters that have already been negotiated.

Zagreb is demanding, among other things, compensation for former prisoners held in Montenegrin camps during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s, clarification of the fate of Croatians who have been missing since that time, and more rigorous prosecution of war crimes.

There are also disputes over the precise maritime boundary between the two countries. In addition, Croatia is demanding payment of about €2.4 billion (about $2.6 billion) for assets that belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, the army of the former Yugoslavia to which both countries belonged before its breakup in the early 1990s.

Montenegro has already responded to some of Croatia's demands, including those concerning compensation for former prisoners. Others, such as the one relating to the assets of the Yugoslav People's Army, are disputed.

It is clear that Croatia's list of demands is also driven by domestic politics. No government in Zagreb can afford to appear compliant on issues relating to the Croatian War of Independence (1991–95).

Moreover, moderate conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic, who is regularly accused in Croatia of being too pro-EU, can use the dispute to portray himself as a staunch defender of national interests.

After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU in June 2022 granted Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova EU candidate status through an accelerated procedure as a gesture of solidarity.

Many EU member states have reservations about Ukraine joining the bloc quickly. Nevertheless, only Hungary, under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, adopted an obstructive stance.

Ostensibly, Hungary's obstruction was about getting Ukraine to improve the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia in western Ukraine. But Orban used the matter for domestic political purposes and as an election campaign issue, portraying Ukraine as a "mafia state."

In an effort to appeal to widespread anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Hungary, the country's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, has also adopted a tough stance on Ukraine.

Nevertheless, Magyar's government lifted several temporary blocks on the opening of new negotiating chapters after the Ukrainian parliament passed a law in early October strengthening the educational rights of national minorities.

No EU candidate country has suffered as much or as long from veto politics as North Macedonia: It was granted EU candidate status in 2005 but only began accession negotiations in July 2022.

Greece blocked the start of negotiations for 13 years because it objected to the name "Republic of Macedonia," as the country was previously known, and accused its neighbor of laying territorial claims to the region of Macedonia in northern Greece.

The dispute was settled in 2018 through a compromise that saw the country change its name to the Republic of North Macedonia the following year.

But just as the path to accession negotiations seemed clear, Bulgaria blocked the opening of talks in November 2020.

Bulgaria regards the Macedonian language as a dialect of Bulgarian and disputes the existence of a distinct Macedonian nation.

Here, too, domestic Bulgarian politics is ultimately a factor.

Former Bulgarian President and current Prime Minister Rumen Radev, for example, fueled the escalation with North Macedonia to enhance his political profile.

Although Serbia has been negotiating EU accession since 2014, little progress has been made.

In July, when the country was still led by President Aleksandar Vucic, no less than eight EU member states — including Croatia — opposed opening further negotiating chapters with Serbia.

While the main reservations relate to democratic shortcomings, deficiencies in the rule of law and corruption in Serbia, Croatia also has its own disputes with its eastern neighbor.

These concern the 1991–95 war, including missing persons, war crimes, minority rights and differing interpretations of history. Relations are also strained by nationalist rhetoric on both sides.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Whether the election victory of the Student List in Belgrade in late October , after almost two years of anti-government and anti-corruption protests, will change this situation is impossible to say.

The EU opened accession negotiations with Albania, which has been an EU candidate since 2014, in July 2022.

Albania could become the bloc's next new member after Montenegro. However, Greece has repeatedly threatened (most recently in June) to block the accession process unless the rights of its Greek minority, particularly their property rights, are adequately protected.

In light of all this, Brussels has long been debating a reform of the accession process and the EU veto system.

In early October, the European Commission proposed that decisions to open negotiations with candidate countries be made by qualified majority rather than unanimously. It also proposed that new EU members would be required to give up the right to veto decisions in certain policy areas altogether for a specified period.

The problem with these proposed reforms is that they would themselves have to be adopted unanimously. In other words, any member state could veto the reform.
